I.label: Ⅰ
I.lead: 次の英文を読み、設問A・B・Cに答えよ。
I.source_note: Based on The Salt in the Data: How Health Headlines Mislead Us by Margaret Ellsworth (adapted).
paragraphs: Every few weeks a new headline promises that some everyday food will either rescue your health or quietly destroy it. Coffee is a poison on Monday and a medicine by Friday; eggs are condemned one year and praised the next; a single glass of wine is dangerous and protective in the very same newspaper. Readers who try to obey this shifting advice end up bewildered, and [[BL:1]] the scientists nor the reporters seem eager to accept the blame. The real problem is not that researchers are dishonest. It is that the studies behind these stories are far weaker than the confident language used to describe [[BL:2]].

Most nutrition research relies [[BL:3]] observation rather than experiment. Investigators cannot lock thousands of people in a laboratory for decades and dictate every meal, so instead they recruit volunteers, ask them what they usually eat, and then follow their health over many years. The human [[BL:4]] in these studies are never assigned a diet by the researchers; they choose one for themselves, according to taste, income, culture, and habit. That single fact, easy to overlook, [[UL:ア=undermines]] almost every dramatic claim that later appears in print. When people select their own way of living, the groups being compared come to differ in countless hidden ways that have nothing to do with the food under examination. By the time the data are gathered, a simple label such as 'coffee drinker' can conceal an entire way of life.

Consider a study reporting that people who eat plenty of leafy vegetables live noticeably longer than those who do not. The headline practically writes itself: greens prevent death. But stop and ask who actually piles spinach and kale onto their plates. Very often they are wealthier, exercise more, smoke less, sleep better, and visit their doctors regularly. Any one of these advantages could [[UL:イ=account for]] the longer lives, quite apart from the vegetables. Statisticians call such lurking influences confounders, and although careful analysts try to [[UL:ウ=adjust for]] them with elaborate mathematics, no calculation can remove a factor that was never measured in the first place. Wealth, in particular, buys not only better food but also cleaner air, safer work, and lower stress. The neat comparison is therefore [[UL:エ=at odds with]] the tidy story of cause and effect that the headline tells.

There is a subtler trap as well, one that researchers call the healthy-user effect. People who dutifully follow a single piece of medical advice tend to follow many others, so the apparent benefit of any one food may simply [[UL:オ=boil down to]] a general willingness to look after oneself. A vitamin supplement, a breakfast cereal, even a particular brand of yogurt can appear protective merely because the conscientious, cautious sort of person is the one most likely to buy them. Statistical software cannot see intentions, and intentions are precisely what drive both the diet and the apparent good health. Untangling this web of overlapping habits is enormously difficult, and honest scientists readily admit that a lone observational study can rarely [[UL:カ=rule out]] every rival explanation.

None of this means that such research is worthless. Observation is frequently the only ethical way to study what humans eat over a lifetime, and the patterns it uncovers can point toward questions worth testing far more rigorously in controlled trials. The real danger lies in the translation from laboratory to living room. A cautious sentence about a modest statistical association becomes, by the time it reaches the front page, a blunt command about what you may and may not put in your mouth. If a finding genuinely matters, it will be [[BL:5]] again and again by different teams using different methods; a result that flares up once and then quietly vanishes deserves patience, not obedience. Science advances by repetition, not by revelation.

So the next time a headline orders you to swear off some ingredient or to swallow another by the handful, pause before rearranging your entire kitchen. Ask whether the people in the study were assigned their diet or merely chose it, and whether anyone else has managed to repeat the work. The single most valuable habit a reader can cultivate is not a fashionable new diet at all, but a steady willingness to greet every miraculous claim with measured doubt.

II.label: Ⅱ
II.lead: 次の英文を読み、設問A〜Cに答えなさい。
II.source_note: Based on Smoke and Certainty: A Short History of Tobacco and Public Health by Margaret E. Holloway (adapted).
paragraphs: For much of the twentieth century, the cigarette occupied a curious place in everyday life. It was marketed as a mark of sophistication, and physicians themselves appeared in advertisements praising one brand [[BL:1]] another. Glossy magazines carried images of film stars exhaling elegant curls of smoke, and the gesture came to signify glamour, independence, and calm. Few ordinary people suspected that the pleasant habit might carry a lethal cost, [[BL:2]] did the tobacco firms have any incentive to raise the alarm. Smoking was woven so deeply into social ritual that questioning it seemed almost impolite.

The first cracks in this comfortable consensus appeared in statistics rather than in the clinic. During the 1930s and 1940s, doctors in several countries noticed a puzzling rise in cases of lung cancer, a disease that had once been rare. The numbers were hard to explain away, for they climbed year after year in men who had reached middle age. To many observers, [[UL:ア=the culprit]] seemed obvious: the fumes of automobiles or the tar of newly paved roads. Yet a handful of researchers suspected that the answer lay closer to home, in the pocket of nearly every adult man.

In 1950, two British scientists set out to test the idea with rigor. Rather than relying on vague impressions, they interviewed hundreds of hospital patients, comparing those with lung cancer to those without. The pattern that emerged was unmistakable: the heavier the smoking, the greater the risk. To silence critics who argued that sick people might simply misremember their habits, the pair then followed thousands of healthy doctors for years, recording who smoked and who fell ill. This second approach, tracking healthy volunteers into the future, was far harder to dismiss, since no one could accuse a well person of inventing a diagnosis that had not yet occurred. The verdict, published over the following decade, [[BL:3]] little room for doubt.

Even so, translating evidence into action proved painfully slow. The tobacco industry funded its own studies, [[BL:4]] the science and insisting that the link was mere coincidence. For a time, the public heard two competing voices — one urging caution, the other counseling calm — and many chose to believe whichever was more convenient. Governments, wary of losing tax revenue and of appearing to lecture their citizens, hesitated for years. It was not until warning labels, advertising bans, and steep taxes were introduced that smoking rates began their long decline. What finally shifted the balance was not a single dramatic discovery but the slow accumulation of proof, [[BL:5]] [[UL:イ=at the public's disposal]] through decades of relentless campaigning.

The story of tobacco offers [[UL:ウ=a sobering lesson]] about how societies come to accept uncomfortable truths. Knowledge alone, it turns out, rarely changes behavior on its own; it must be carried forward by institutions willing to act upon it, even at a cost to themselves. Progress, in other words, depended less on the brilliance of a single mind than on the patience of a society learning to trust its own measurements.

III.label: Ⅲ
III.lead: 次の英文を読み、あとの設問(A・B・C)に答えなさい。
III.source_note: Based on The Driverless Horizon by Malcolm A. Webb (Ashford Press, 2021)
paragraphs: For more than a century, the automobile has been guided entirely by human hands. That long-standing arrangement is now being called into question. Engineers across the globe are racing to build cars that can [[UL:1=carry out]] the entire task of driving with no human input at all. These vehicles rely on a dense web of sensors, cameras, and software that together [[DU:ア=interpret the surrounding world far faster than any human eye could manage]]. Supporters insist that such machines will eventually make our roads dramatically safer.

Their confidence rests on a simple statistic: human mistakes [[UL:2=account for]] the overwhelming majority of traffic deaths. A computer never drinks, never grows sleepy at the wheel, nor does it glance down at a buzzing phone. In theory, then, handing control to a machine should remove the single largest cause of danger on the road. [[DU:イ=It is precisely this promise of saving tens of thousands of lives each year that keeps investors pouring money into the field]].

Yet the technology is far from flawless. Machines can be baffled by situations that a young child would grasp in an instant. A plastic bag drifting across a lane, a police officer waving cars through a red light, or heavy snow that hides the road markings—each can puzzle a system that was never trained on that precise scene. Because such rare events are so hard to anticipate, most researchers believe it will be a long time before we can safely [[UL:3=do away with]] the steering wheel altogether. In the meantime, cars are being designed to hand control back to a human whenever they meet something they cannot understand—[[DU:ウ=an awkward compromise that assumes a distracted passenger can suddenly become an alert driver within a second or two]].

There is also the thorny question of blame. When a self-driving car causes a crash, who is at fault: the owner, the manufacturer, or the engineer who wrote the code? Lawmakers have been slow to respond, and the few rules that do exist differ sharply from one country to the next. [[UL:4=On the whole]], society has not yet decided how much risk it is willing to accept in exchange for the convenience these vehicles promise.

Despite these hurdles, the direction of travel seems clear. Delivery companies are already testing driverless trucks on quiet highways, and a handful of cities now allow robotaxis to operate within carefully mapped zones. Whether or not ordinary drivers welcome the shift, the coming decades will almost certainly see the human driver pushed steadily toward the margins—much as the horse was long ago displaced by the engine.
